note: One loop, the I–vi–ii–V in C, comped with shell voicings three ways: short chords on 2 and 4, the root alone on 1 and 3 under them, then each shell picked apart in eighths. The shells are drawn in a chord-shapes with their frets, the chords are counted the long way once, every strum-along carries the pattern its text describes, and the tempo is moves.

exercise.title: Comp the I–vi–ii–V with shells
exercise.why: A shell is only the root, 3rd and 7th, so the picking hand can play it short, split the root from the other two notes, or pick it apart, and the same four chords make three different parts.

cells.text: Cmaj7 is the 1st chord in the key of C, Am7 the 6th, Dm7 the 2nd and G7 the 5th: in that order they make the I–vi–ii–V. Below are their shell voicings. Press a chord box below to hear one.

Press Play below to start the metronome. After a bar of count-in, the lit box shows the chord to play. Strum each shell on beats 2 and 4, and lift your fretting fingers a little to stop the sound short.
Practice until the next shell is under your fingers before its beat 2 comes.

Press Play below to start the metronome again. Pick the root, the lowest note of the shell, alone on beats 1 and 3, then strum the 3rd and 7th together on beats 2 and 4.
If the root comes late after a change, keep the strums on 2 and 4 going and catch the root on the next beat 1.

Press Play below to start the metronome, a little slower. Pick one note of the shell on every stroke the lit box shows: up from the root through the three notes, then back down, and let them ring.
Practice until it is in your muscle memory: your picking hand finds the string of each root without you looking.
